newsitem.title: USA: Nintendo cuts game player prices.
newsitem.headline: Nintendo cuts game player prices.

text.p: Nintendo of America Monday cut prices of its popular Nintendo 64 game player to $149.95 from $199.95 in response to a similar price cut from arch-rival Sony Corp. setting up the possibility of even lower prices for the critical Christmas season.
Nintendo of America, a unit of Japanese video maker Nintendo Co Ltd, made the price cut close on the heels of Sony, which cut prices of its popular Playstation to $149 from $199 earlier in the month.
"The price cuts really help demand," said Larry Marcus, analyst at Alex Brown. "It's a sign that the current video game market is robust and is expected to continue to be so."
"It's a seasonally slow period of the year so probably more important than the near term boost is the potential for prices to go even lower by Christmas," he added.
Marcus said he expects prices for the Nintendo 64 and Sony's Playstation may dip to the $99 to $119 range. Other industry watchers also see prices being slashed.
"I think most people expect prices to be in the $99 price range by Christmas," Bear Stearns analyst Paul Rogers said.
"It's good news for software developers ... because lower prices lead to higher unit sales and that's really what drives growth for entertainment software vendors," he added.

Nintendo, which introduced Nintendo 64 in time for Christmas 1996, dominates the market for children under 14 due to its better adventure games while Sony, which released its Playstation the prior year, has dominating the older market because it has better fighting games.
Some analysts are concerned that Nintendo may see its market share eroded because it's cartridge-based games are more expensive to produce that the CD system employed by Sony and others.
"(Nintendo) have a pretty big hurdle," said Keith Benjamin, an analyst at Robertson Stephens & Co.
"The technology is reasonably impressive but the pricing of the cartridges and the business model don't seem to be a recipe for long-term success. Sony has the momentum."
Nintendo cartridges cost third party game developers over $30, plus royalties to Nintendo, per unit to make whereas the CD technology used by Sony costs less than $5 a unit to make.
That means software developers are much more likely to tailor their best games to the Sony system where profit margins are much higher, Benjamin said.

"For people to want to buy the (Nintendo) hardware they want to believe there is a lot of software available and the long-term success of any of these platforms is their ability to attract game developers," Benjamin said..
"What Nintendo has to do long-term is come up with a CD system, which is not going to be easy," he added.
"(Nintendo) sold 3.5 million units in the December quarter worldwide," he said. "They're off to a very fast start, it doesn't look like having a cartridge and not a CD is holding them back."
Larry Marcus is also unconcerned about the high price of making games for Nintendo.

"The future of the cartridge technology is very bright," he said. "People in the industry try to focus on now expensive these cartridges are but from a consumer standpoint what really matters is now great the game is."
